newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian markets hit by fresh Suharto rumours.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian markets hit by fresh Suharto rumours.

text.p: Indonesia's financial markets were rattled again on Friday following a fresh round of rumours about President Suharto's health, brokers and dealers said.

The rupiah fell almost three points to the dollar to 2,406.5 at midday on unfounded rumours that 75-year old Suharto, who has ruled Indonesia for more than 30 years, planned to undergo a medical check-up in Germany.
Presidential palace officials denied any such move.
"There is no such plan and there's no indication at all the president will have a new medical check-up," one source told Reuters.

"It's not true he will travel to Germany for a check-up," another palace source confirmed. Witnesses said Suharto attended official functions and Friday prayers at a mosque in the presidential palace grounds.
By mid-afternoon, the rupiah had recovered to 2,405/06 against the dollar against an opening of 2,404.5/05.5.
Stocks were less affected, but prices were depressed with the composite index shedding 0.32 percent to 639.58 points at midsession after dropping almost two percent on Thursday.

The rupiah, coming under sustained upward pressure against the dollar due to strong economic fundamentals, started falling on Wednesday in New York and London following an unfounded report that Suharto was suffering from a minor heart ailment.
Foreign Minister Ali Alatas denied the rumours on Thursday. Several Jakarta-based newspapers published stories and pictures on Friday of Suharto at official ceremonies.
The rupiah tumbled 22 points in New York from the Jakarta close on Wednesday. It has since recovered but continues to be susceptible to pressure.

Dealers said the weakening of the rupiah on Friday was not substantial although the market remained jittery and sensitive to any fresh rumours linked to Suharto's health. They said political issues would continue to play a strong role in the financial markets ahead of the May 29 parliamentary elections.
"Elections and politics in general have become more of an issue in the run-up to the May election," Daragh Maher, an economist at ING Baring Securities, told Reuters.
"The rupiah will be vulnerable to any rumour in relation to the (presidential) succession or Suharto's health," Maher said.

Suharto went to Germany for a medical check-up last year and was declared healthy for the man of his age. He is widely expected to run for a seventh term as president in the March 1998 presidential elections.
Desmond Supple, head of research for Asian currencies with BZW Barclays in Singapore, said the main concern was politics because there was no plan in place for a successor to Suharto.
"The political system is still a one-man band. It relies on him with no real basis for a succession at the moment," he said.
But both Maher and Supple remained positive on Indonesia.
"Look at the economic fundamentals, all of which seem to be working quite happily in Indonesia's favour," Maher said.
Supple said the political issue was the key risk because the economy as a whole was looking good.

Maher added volatility should decrease as the presidential elections approached, because there would be a clearer indication of whether Suharto would stand and whether he would put in place any potential successor.

"Therefore you could potentially see less volatility rather than more," he said, adding the rupiah was expected to depreciate at the same Central Bank-guided rate over the medium-term and possibly a bit slower.
"But within that you have a period of volatility," he said.
